newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Export growth to squeeze UK Aug trade gap.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Export growth to squeeze UK Aug trade gap.

text.p: Britain's trade gap with the rest of the world probably narrowed modestly in August thanks to a better export performance with countries both inside and outside the European Union, analysts said.
But the pound's recent rally may mean the trade picture deteriorated in September as UK exports grew more expensive.

Figures for worldwide trade in August and non-European Union trade for September are due on Friday at 0830 GMT. The Reuters consensus forecast suggests the global trade deficit narrowed to 1.0 bln stg in August from 1.229 billion stg in July.
But it also predicted September's deficit between the UK and non-EU countries widened to 730 million stg from 499 million.
"Figures have already been released showing a drop in the UK's trade gap with non-EU countries (in August)," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.
"We expect this to be accompanied by a drop in the trade gap with EU countries to about 300 million stg."
Data out last month showed the deficit between the UK and non-EU countries narrowed to 499 million stg in August from 688 million stg in July.

Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, agreed. "The global deficit looks almost certain to narrow again in August given the sharp fall in the deficit with non-EU countries and we have allowed for a narrowing in the EU deficit to about 300 million (from 541 million stg in July)."
A welcome feature of recent trade data has been the strength of exports which have held up despite the fact that key trading partners have been beset by sluggish economic growth.
"The key strength has been concentrated in exports to outside the EU which have clearly benefited from the pick up in activity in the U.S. this year," said Loynes.
But there is a danger that with the U.S. economy set to slow modestly in the next few months, this export growth will slow.
And sterling's recent appreciation will also make British goods less attractively priced abroad.
The pound has gained over six percent on a trade-weighted basis since early August.

Both the Confederation of British Industry and British Chambers of Commerce have suggested sterling has not yet reached a level to worry exporters, but any further rise is sure to have an impact on British competitiveness.

Although imports are expected to grow as the economic recovery gathers pace and the pound's rally pushes import prices down, in the short term at least the strength of the pound will help mask the impact of climbing import volumes on the trading balance.
"With the stock cycle about to turn and activity accelerating, we expect import growth will pick up in the next few months," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
"But its impact on the trade deficit will be mitigated by a favourable movement in the terms of trade thanks to a firmer pound." -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7715
